p.t: In short
p.s: Account suspensions, appeals and Google support

p.t: Google can **block** your store account (a suspension), but a block is not a deletion, and most blocks can be fixed.
Most blocks come from **mismatches**: your store's shipping, tax, phone, prices or policies differ from what Google has on file.
Never make up a product **barcode number (GTIN), and never open a new account** to get around a block.
Fix the cause first, then send a calm, factual **appeal** (a formal request for review).
**Keep calling or chatting with Google** until a person who can help answers. Follow up on the same case with proof.
**Do not open a new Google Ads account** while the old one is suspended. Work on the old account first.
**Do not hand your ads to an agency** until your own store makes a profit and you know your starting results.
Sources disagree on some routes. Check the year of each piece of advice before you act on it.
Account suspensions, appeals and Google support
Why accounts get suspended
Google suspends **Merchant Center accounts mainly for five reasons**.
p.h: Merchant center: misrepresentation and data mismatches

p.t:
Merchant Center is Google's tool that holds your product data.
Business information does not match the **website**.
Product **data** is incomplete.

**Required** business information is missing from the website.
Merchant Center **settings** are incomplete.

Products are in **prohibited** categories (product types Google bans).
A suspension is **not a deletion**. The account is only blocked from use.

Suspensions often carry the reason **misrepresentation**. This means Google believes some information is missing or wrong. Suspension notices arrive by email to the business email address set up for the account.
A suspension is a **legitimacy check** (a test of whether your store is real and trustworthy), not a final verdict. Google suspends to protect searchers and to screen out scam or low-quality stores.
New accounts are checked most strictly and are often suspended **almost immediately**. Established accounts can also be suspended after **two years or more** of trading.
Google tightened account security after the e-commerce boom in 2020, so suspensions can also hit **legitimate (real, honest) sellers.**
**A suspension can be reversed, so fix the cause and request reinstatement** (getting the account turned back on) rather than panic.
Common causes of suspension are **shipping or tax information** in Merchant Center that does not match the Shopify store (your store software),
product prices in the catalog (your product list) that do not match the store, missing contact information, and a missing privacy policy.
Missing or inconsistent contact details can cause a contact-information suspension.
The contact page should offer at least **two contact methods**, such as a phone number, an email address or a contact form, plus a privacy policy.
A **currency mismatch** (the money type does not match), missing contact details or a missing privacy policy can flag an account. Fix these and then appeal.
A missing or **unverified** (not confirmed) business phone number in Merchant Center is a recurring trigger for misrepresentation.
Shipping costs, the shipping policy and the privacy policy **URLs (web addresses) in Merchant Center must match what appears in the Shopify store,**
Merchant center: misrepresentation and data mismatches (continued)
p.s: Account suspensions, appeals and Google support

p.t: **because Google bots** (automatic visitors) add products to cart to check this.
Footer social links (links at the bottom of a page) that point to Shopify social pages or to platform home pages, instead of your own profiles, were a known cause of a Merchant Center suspension.
Change them to **your own profiles** or remove them, then resubmit (send again). (Advice from 2023.)
Misrepresentation often comes from **missing policy pages** and content. Make sure the store has all required policies and pages.
Vague or missing wording in shipping and return policies is a common cause of a suspension without a clear reason. Check that both policies are **clear and complete**.
Never **invent** a GTIN (a product's barcode number) or enter a third-party GTIN (a barcode that belongs to someone else) that does not belong to the product.
Google treats a mismatched GTIN as misrepresentation, which can lead to suspension.
A **missing GTIN alone does not cause a misrepresentation suspension. The problem arises only when a wrong** identifier is placed in the GTIN field (the box where the barcode number goes).
A contact detail or policy that differs even slightly from the Merchant Center entry can trigger misrepresentation. Example: a suite number (an office or apartment number) written differently.
Compare address, phone, email and every policy **character by character** with the store.
A Merchant Center suspension can have many causes.
Check the GTIN, verified phone number, shipping, return and privacy policies, and product detail content, and use the **full checklist** before escalating to support (asking a higher level of help).
Installed dropshipping apps alone were not considered a cause of account rejection.
The likely trigger is a **red flag** (a warning sign) on the store that a Google bot detects as dropshipping (selling products that a supplier ships for you).
Blocking Google's **checkout crawler (an automatic visitor that checks the payment page) to hide abandoned checkouts (carts customers left before paying) also leads to automatic feed** suspension.
The feed is your product data file. Do not try to block it.
Test ads with fake URLs or non-existent websites can get a **Google Ads** account suspended. Google Ads is Google's paid ad tool. Ads must point to the business website linked to the account.
Google Ads: account-Level reasons
p.s: Account suspensions, appeals and Google support

p.t:
Google Ads accounts are suspended for specific reasons:
**Incorrect** business information.
**Multiple accounts tied to the same business or personal information, including old dormant** (unused) accounts after a prior suspension.
A **payment method** flagged as fraudulent (possible fraud) or previously bounced (refused).
**Ads** that point to a URL (web address) other than the business website, or to a website that does not exist.
A Google Ads suspension applies to the **whole** advertiser account and every related account.
While suspended, you cannot open new accounts, and ads stop running on Search (Google's results page), search partner sites and the Display Network (Google's network of other websites that show ads)
at the same time. A store that relies on one paid channel can lose all paid traffic (visitors from ads) at once.
Google can flag an ad account as **restricted** in a country where the advertiser does not sell or advertise. This is usually an automated error (a computer mistake).

For suspected **bot clicks (fake clicks from automatic programs), contact Google support by live chat** (chatting with a person on the support site) for the recommended course of action before relying
on a click-blocking tool alone.
A Google Ads suspension for suspicious payment activity is usually caused by **billing details** (the name and address on the payment method) that do not match the account.
This is covered in the appeal steps below.
Circumventing systems and linked accounts
p.s: Account suspensions, appeals and Google support

p.t: The **circumventing systems** suspension (trying to get around a platform's rules) usually occurs
when Google believes a new account was opened after a previous account was closed.
The circumventing flag often appears when a previously suspended account used the **same** billing address, credit card or website as a new account.
Creating a new account to get around a policy triggers this flag.
Google can link new ad accounts to earlier ones through **IP address (your internet address), cookies (small files a website saves in your browser), name, address and card details.**
**Creating a new ad account after a suspension therefore usually fails**.
A suspension on one platform does not automatically affect other platforms. Accounts on Microsoft, Facebook, TikTok, Pinterest and Instagram can keep running.
Using **agency accounts** (accounts run by an outside ad company) to circumvent bans on Google Merchant Center is not recommended. It can lead to a cycle of banned accounts and costs a lot of money.
Only use **.com** domains (web addresses ending in.com) for the store.
Do not switch to a.store or.us domain to fix a Google Ads policy problem, because changing domains to get around a flag can look like circumventing systems.
The circumventing flag can be a **false flag** (a wrong warning) when a new account was opened after a previously closed account.
If you never had an earlier account, appeal the suspension instead of creating a new one.

First Steps
p.s: Account suspensions, appeals and Google support

p.t: 1. **Do not reply immediately**, and do not reply in anger.
2. Read the suspension reason in Google's email. It may be a **warning** giving 7 days to fix the issue, or an immediate suspension.
3. Check that the business information in the account is complete.
4. Make sure the website follows the business launch checklist (a list of what a store needs before it goes live).
5. Check product data in the feed for **disapproved** products (products Google rejected) and missing attributes (missing product detail fields).

6. Make sure **shipping, tax, phone number** and other account information match the website exactly.
7. **Delete** old, unused Google Ads accounts.
8. Submit a detailed, neutral response through the form or avenue in Google's email, explaining what was checked and changed and asking for a review.
9. Expect a review within **one to two days**, sometimes up to a week.
10. Replies asking for unsuspension must be neutral and factual. An angry or terse (short and curt) reply makes the problem worse and delays the review.
11. When a Merchant Center issue is unclear, respond calmly, check the official Google policy pages, and ask an expert or coach rather than attempting a risky fix alone.

Avoiding New Accounts
**Do not start** a new Google Ads account while an existing one is suspended (switched off by Google).
p.h: Rules against opening a replacement account

p.t: Creating a second account to get around a suspension is treated as circumventing the system (dodging the rules) and can lead to a permanent block.
After a Google Ads account suspension, **do not create** a new Google Ads account. A new one is usually suspended as well, and Google may cite circumvention of policy.
Opening a new ad account right after a suspension can get it blocked or suspended again **within minutes**.
**Work through the appeal** (the formal request to reverse the decision) on the existing account rather than repeatedly creating replacement accounts.
A new account with a different email and card may still be linked if it is opened from the same computer or **IP address** (the number that identifies your internet connection).
Creating a second Merchant Center account to get around a disapproval causes more problems. **Fix the disapproval** and request review instead. (Advice from 2023.)
**Do not delete** the account and create a new one with the same email, because that is flagged as circumventing policies.
**Do not run a new account with the same card or domain** (your website address) as the suspended one. (See the conditional route below.)

Google Ads agencies tend to be maintenance-focused rather than proactively scaling because the platform requires more campaign setup work per testing cycle.
**Clarify scaling expectations upfront** and map deliverables week by week.
Google Ads return on ad spend is claimed in the source to be strong, around **4x to 7x** in typical cases. Outsourced Google Ads management in the source cost about 1,500 dollars per month.
A good agency brief sets a measurable goal: **keep a 13X return** on ad spend while raising monthly spend from 1,000 to 2,000 dollars, or raise return from 13X to 15X at the same spend.
Without a baseline, an agency has nothing to be judged against.
Judge the performance of an outsourced Google Ads manager by **ROAS trend**, not spend alone. A flat or weak ROAS at a relatively small ad budget should be improved before the budget is raised.

When an agency is paid a fixed monthly fee, **check whether the ROAS justifies it**. A 10x ROAS on 2,000 dollars monthly spend was judged acceptable for a new account, but needs to improve as spend grows.
